authors: Victor Cui; Qian Xiang; Jiatao Li; Jianqi Zhang
affiliations: Conrad School of Entrepreneurship and Business University of Waterloo Waterloo Ontario Canada; School of Finance and Economics Guangdong Polytechnic Normal University Guangzhou China; School of Business and Management Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Clear Water Bay Hong Kong; Lingnan College Sun Yat‐sen University Guangzhou China
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Anecdotes suggest that multinational enterprises (MNEs) from weak intellectual property rights (IPR) regimes often leapfrog to technological leadership by recruiting talent in advanced host countries. Yet whether—and how—such a strategy works remains unclear. Using data on 486 MNEs from 29 countries operating in the United States and interviews with skilled inventors, we uncover a paradox in the springboard‐via‐hiring logic: externally, weak home‐country IPR reputation deters skilled inventors from joining, limiting recruitment; internally, even when talent is hired, home‐country‐imprinted IPR routines constrain post‐hire learning, yielding incremental improvements. These effects are mitigated by firm‐specific exposure to host‐country patent infringement litigation. Our research suggests that springboard‐via‐hiring is institution‐based, contingent on both home‐ and host‐country IPR regimes. These findings offer implications for technology policy and MNEs' strategy amid geopolitical tension. Managerial Summary Can multinational enterprises (MNEs) from weak intellectual property rights (IPR) regimes leapfrog by hiring technical talent in advanced economies? Evidence on 486 MNEs from 29 countries operating in the US high‐technology sector suggests: weaker home‐country IPR reputations make it harder to attract skilled inventors; even after hiring, home‐imprinted IPR routines can constrain recruits' knowledge transfer, often steering outcomes toward incremental improvements. These home‐country constraints are, however, mitigated by firm‐specific exposure to US patent infringement litigation. The springboard‐via‐hiring strategy is thus institution‐based, contingent on both home‐ and host‐country IPR regimes. We accordingly offer advice on technology policy and global R&D strategies for host‐country governments and MNEs amid geopolitical tension.

title: Does FinTech Innovation Improve Traditional Banks’ Operating Efficiency and Risk? Empirical Evidence from Patent Filings
authors: Libing Fang; Xindan Li; Avanidhar Subrahmanyam; Ke Zhang
affiliations: School of Management and Engineering, Jiangsu Key Laboratory of Digital Finance, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu 210093, China; Anderson Graduate School of Management, University of California at Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California 90095; School of Digital Economics and Management, Nanjing University, Suzhou, Jiangsu 215163, China
abstract: We empirically examine the link between bank-specific innovations in financial technology (FinTech) and traditional banks’ fundamentals. We propose a new measure for FinTech innovation as the textual similarity of banks’ patent filings to standard FinTech policy documents. We show that FinTech innovation implies enhanced efficiency, profitability, and operating capacity (e.g., cost management, funding and lending activity). FinTech also ameliorates banks’ risk measures, including overall risk (Z-score), the liquidity, and nonperforming loan ratios. Our heterogeneity analysis suggests that banks with stronger managerial capacity and higher labor intensity derive moderately greater benefits from FinTech innovations. Further analysis reveals that FinTech-driven lending expansions focus on unsecured and low-risk loans, with technological specializations in cloud computing. We also find supportive evidence that expanding innovation in artificial intelligence and blockchain can yield performance gains to commercial banks. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. title: Payout Taxes Matter: The Financing R&D Mechanism
authors: James R. Brown; Gustav Martinsson
affiliations: Adam C. Sinn ‘00 Department of Finance, Mays Business School, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas 77843; Stockholm Business School, Stockholm University, Stockholm, SE-106 91 Sweden; and Sweden and Swedish House of Finance, SE-113 50 Stockholm, Sweden
abstract: Higher taxes on corporate payouts increase the cost of financing with stock issues. As a result, corporate investments that rely on external equity financing should be particularly sensitive to payout tax rates. A large literature shows that firms rely extensively on stock issues to fund research and development (R&D), suggesting that the financing of R&D is a potentially important microlevel mechanism linking payout taxation with real corporate activity. We document a robust negative association between dividend tax rates and firm R&D investment in a broad sample of developed countries between 2000 and 2019. The negative relation between dividend taxes and R&D is concentrated in equity-dependent firms in high-R&D industries. R&D is more sensitive to dividend tax rates in countries with stock market–based financial systems. Dividend taxes are less important for investment in physical capital than for R&D. Higher dividend taxes are associated with less corporate financing with stock issues, particularly in firms with low internal cash flow. Our study highlights the importance of focusing on equity-dependent activities and firms to evaluate the real consequences of payout taxation. This paper was accepted by Gustavo Manso, finance. title: A Unified Resilience Evaluation Framework for Markov‐Type Based Multi‐State Systems
authors: Meiyan Li; Bei Wu; Nikolaos Limnios; Xiangyu Qin
affiliations: School of Management Northwestern Polytechnical University Xi'an China; Laboratory of Applied Mathematics of Compiègne University of Technology of Compiègne Compiègne France
abstract: ABSTRACT Resilience has emerged as a fundamental attribute in the design and management of complex systems, reflecting the growing recognition that systems must not only resist disruptions but also recover effectively. While conceptual advances have been substantial, the quantification of resilience in a manner that integrates both capacities remains an open challenge. To address this gap, this paper introduces a unified resilience evaluation framework for multi‐state systems exposed to single or multiple hazards, whose performance evolution is characterized using four Markov‐type models: Markov chains, semi‐Markov chains, Markov processes, and semi‐Markov processes. Two resilience dimensions, namely absorptive and restorative resilience, are defined to quantify the capacity of the system to withstand disruptions and restore functionality, respectively. For each dimension, both static and dynamic metrics are proposed to capture pathway‐based probabilities and time‐dependent behaviors. Analytical formulas are derived for all resilience metrics and subsequently verified through simulation‐based algorithms. The applicability of the models and metrics is demonstrated through two case studies: a building portfolio and a nuclear power plant, both subjected to earthquake hazards. The findings illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed fram ework in characterizing multi‐state system resilience, with practical implications for system design and risk management.

title: When Critical Roads Fail: Nonlinear Impacts of Flooding on Network Connectivity and Community Resilience
authors: Shun Cao; Hiroki Sayama; Changqing Cheng
affiliations: School of Management State University of New York Binghamton New York USA; School of Systems Science and Industrial Engineering State University of New York Binghamton New York USA; Waseda Innovation Lab Waseda University Tokyo Japan
abstract: ABSTRACT Flooding is among the most disruptive hazards to community access, severing mobility lifelines and isolating residential areas from essential services. This study addresses that gap by integrating an inundation model with percolation analysis to evaluate how floods reshape network connectivity, efficiency, and service accessibility. With the illustrative example of Broome County, NY, we simulated progressive road inundation based on elevation and traced cascading effects on network connectivity, efficiency, and service access. Results revealed that while fewer than 20% of roads are directly inundated, the modeled network exhibits an abrupt transition within an approximate elevation band near 263–264 m under the present modeling assumptions. At this threshold, the failure of a few cross‐valley connectors fragments the network, reduces efficiency by about 60%, disconnects more than 80% of the predefined analyzed origin–destination pairs, and cuts off access to emergency services. Accessibility loss follows a service‐specific sequence, with police access deteriorating first, followed by fire stations and hospitals. A qualitative comparison with historical impact data provides contextual support for the broad spatial patterns produced by the model. Because the framework requires only digital elevation models and open‐source road data, it is computationally efficient and globally transferable. By reframing flood impacts as nonlinear percolation processes, it provides network‐level insights and practical guidance for protecting strategic bottlenecks and sustaining community access under extreme events.

title: Toward More Resilient Community: Unveiling Information Dissemination Mode of Disaster Risk by a Social Network Approach
authors: Feiting Gao; Li Peng; Damin Zhou; Juntao Sun; Pei Huang
affiliations: College of Geography and Resources Sichuan Normal University Chengdu China; Key Laboratory of Land Resources Evaluation and Monitoring in Southwest Ministry of Education Sichuan Normal University Chengdu China
abstract: ABSTRACT The timely, clear, and accurate dissemination of geo‐disaster information to the public is a critical component of climate adaptation and disaster response strategies. However, behavioral inertia and the amplification of misinformation pose major challenges to risk communication in rural areas, hindering effective climate resilience building. In this study, survey data were collected from 536 rural households in the Longmen Mountain region in southwest China, which is an area frequently threatened by geohazards exacerbated by changing climate patterns. Social network analysis (SNA) was applied to explore how formal and informal communication channels influence household response behaviors. A novel channel–behavior model was developed to analyze the differences in information dissemination for risk communication and rumor propagation. The results showed that formal communication channels such as village broadcasting dominated risk communication and were more likely to trigger collective action, serving as a vital policy instrument for local governance. In contrast, rumor propagation was primarily driven by informal communication channels such as the internet. Communities were divided into two specific types: passively receptive and risk‐accumulating. Passively receptive communities showed high internal cohesion and rapid norm dissemination while risk‐accumulating communities exhibited fragmented structures that impeded information dissemination and increased vulnerability. The results demonstrate the utility of integrating SNA into human‐environment geography and provide actionable insights for designing spatially sensitive, community‐tailored risk communication policies to enhance climate resilience in rural China.

title: When Human Nature and AI Collide: Identifying Emergent Biases in Risk Management Through Netnography
authors: Helmi Issa
affiliations: AI and Decision Sciences ESSCA School of Management Angers France
abstract: ABSTRACT As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support expert judgment in risk management, the interaction between human and machine generates unintended consequences in the form of emergent biases that distort decision‐making and undermine risk assessments. Taking human–AI teaming as the unit of analysis, this study investigates how collaborative judgment produces biases that neither human error nor software failure alone can explain. Through a netnographic analysis of publicly available podcasts, complemented by three documented case studies, it identifies a cascading, self‐reinforcing cycle of emergent biases (AI Washing [macro‐organizational], Validation [meso‐behavioral], and Off‐Loading [micro‐cognitive]) and the structural interventions (independent benchmarking, temporal separation, and vendor/resource decentralization) positioned at each juncture of that cycle. In doing so, the study defines a new category of risk arising specifically from the relationship between human and AI systems, responds to urgent calls in the risk management literature, and offers organizations a preliminary calibration mechanism for interrupting the bias cascade in AI‐augmented decision environments.

title: Order‐of‐Magnitude Assessment of Strategies to Reduce Risks to Residential Electricity Customers From Tropical Cyclones
authors: Maryam Hamidi; M. Granger Morgan
affiliations: Department of Engineering and Public Policy Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Power distribution systems face increasing risks from tropical cyclones (TCs or hurricanes), which can cause prolonged outages and serious social and economic impacts. While there are models to assess distribution system resilience, they are typically complex and highly location specific. Many smaller utilities, such as co‐ops, lack the resources to develop such frameworks and perform detailed analysis to evaluate distribution system resilience strategies such as pole upgrades. In this paper, we illustrate an order‐of‐magnitude approach that employs stochastic simulation using historical hurricane records and power pole fragility curves for wood power poles to estimate the expected value of replacing wood poles with composite poles which bend, but do not break, under hurricane winds. In an illustration of the method applied to the mid‐Atlantic coast, we find that over a 40‐year period replacing wood poles that have been damaged by TCs with composite poles shows substantial economic advantages over replacement with new wood poles. In this illustration, customer density and geographic TC risk emerge as the primary economic drivers, with coastal suburban feeders showing the greatest benefits across the four feeder types modeled. Total 40‐year cost reductions range from about 18% to 37%, reaching $4.7 million in the highest‐risk coastal suburban scenario. We conclude by noting that a similar order‐of‐magnitude strategy could be adapted and used by utilities and others to assess other risks to distribution systems.

title: Occupational Safety and Health Risks of Augmented Reality at Work: A Literature Review and Interview Study
authors: Simone Grassini
affiliations: Department of Psychosocial Science University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Augmented reality (AR) is increasingly used in manufacturing, logistics, construction, energy, and healthcare to provide workers with hands‐free, task‐specific information. The impact of AR on occupational safety and health (OSH) is still being evaluated. This paper reviews the existing literature on AR‐specific OSH risks and looks at how these are experienced and managed at work. A structured literature review (an initial search covering 2016 to 2023 and an update search to October 2026) was combined with semi‐structured interviews with seven experts from OSH consultancy, labor inspection, industrial safety management, AR development, and frontline supervision. The risks fall into four overlapping areas: perceptual and cognitive (attention being drawn to the display, failure to notice hazards, misplaced virtual content, and over‐reliance on guidance), physical and ergonomic (weight of the headset, reduced blink rate and eye strain, motion sickness with moving content, and battery hazards), psychosocial (stress, isolation and deskilling, with very little evidence in the AR‐specific literature), and privacy and security (continuous sensing of workers, co‐workers, and proprietary processes). The quantitative findings indicate that the perceptual, performance and physiological effects studied are measurable during short exposures but that such evidence is often based on small samples and short tasks. The interviewees also identified these risks and raised organizational concerns: Formal risk assessments were rare (recorded in only one deployment), compatibility with personal protective equipment needed to be checked, devices assessed for one application were expected to be reused in others without reassessment, and standardization and certification were uneven. The paper concludes with AR‐specific risk‐assessment items, design principles and governance priorities, and a research agenda.

title: Expert Judgments of Residual Risk in Three New Zealand Rural High‐Speed Work‐Zone Scenarios
authors: Dave Tilton; Jacobus Daniel van der Walt
affiliations: Department of Civil and Natural Resources Engineering University of Canterbury Christchurch New Zealand
abstract: ABSTRACT New Zealand's move from prescribed layouts toward site‐specific work‐zone risk assessment raises questions about the evidence supporting event‐frequency judgments. We elicited distributions from 36 practitioners for event return periods, conditional severities, and risk multipliers in three rural high‐speed work‐zone scenarios. Participants estimated privately before and after facilitated discussion and anonymized feedback. We pooled their distributions with equal weights. Frequency judgments differed by orders of magnitude and were strongly structured by workshop membership. The Christchurch workshop's median participant return periods exceeded the combined median of the other two workshops on all 12 events (median ratio 13); the Auckland workshops were at or below the combined median of the others on all 12 (median ratio 0.05). In a post hoc descriptive comparison, the median between‐workshop share of squared deviations in log return‐period medians rose from 0.25 before scenario discussion and feedback to 0.76 afterward. This does not establish an effect of deliberation. Inconsistent instructions left the multiplier risk quantity unresolved, and one event had conflicting exposure units. Reference questions lacked fixed realized values, preventing calibration, and no configuration‐matched outcomes validated the judgments. The contribution includes documenting closer agreement within these workshops alongside persistent disagreement between them, and diagnosing limits of the elicitation. The estimates are insufficiently validated for operational use. We recommend shared event and exposure definitions, prospective linked records, validation of intermediate measures, and evaluation of assessment methods used in practice.

title: Beyond Events: Infrastructure as Sociomaterial Signals for Knowing Flood Risk in the Present
authors: Noémia Salgado Cunha
affiliations: Miguel Torga Higher Institute Coimbra Portugal
abstract: ABSTRACT Flood risk has predominantly been conceptualized through future‐oriented regimes of anticipation and is typically recognized only as extreme events approach. This article challenges that framing by reconceptualizing risk as a sociomaterial process that becomes empirically legible in the present through recurring patterns embedded in the everyday functioning of infrastructures. Drawing on prolonged field observation, documentary analysis, and engagement with local actors, it introduces the concept of sociomaterial signals of risk, redefines infrastructures as epistemically active artifacts, and develops an understanding of risk grounded in situated interpretations of infrastructural functioning. For disaster studies, this approach expands what counts as evidence for risk governance, supporting earlier and territorially situated forms of intervention. In doing so, the article redefines the conditions under which risk becomes governable, through the stabilization of recurring sociomaterial signals in everyday infrastructural functioning.

title: Epistemic Monoculture in Risk Assessment: Common‐Cause Blind Spots in Human–AI Teaming
authors: Milad Baghersad; C. Derrick Huang
affiliations: Department of Information Technology & Operations Management, College of Business Florida Atlantic University Boca Raton Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The value of redundancy in risk assessment depends not only on individual assessor accuracy, but also on whether assessment errors remain sufficiently independent. This paper studies how human–AI teaming can weaken that independence when multiple assessors rely on the same or similar AI systems. We develop a formal model of AI‐assisted assessors evaluating a common set of hazards. Each assessor combines its own independent judgment with shared AI‐generated advice. The AI signal may contain random error and class‐specific omission bias for hazards that are rare, novel, or poorly represented in the AI system's information environment. The model identifies an accuracy–correlation trade‐off: Greater reliance on AI can reduce individual mean squared error while making assessors' errors more correlated. When AI advice contains omission bias, greater reliance can also pull multiple assessors' estimates below the escalation threshold for the same hazard class. We derive the individual miss probability, the systemic miss probability that all assessors miss a hazard, the diversity dividend, and the homogenization ratio. The results show that evaluating AI assistance only by individual accuracy can be misleading. Even when AI assistance lowers each assessor's miss probability, it can increase the probability that all assessors miss the same hazard if the added correlation in their errors outweighs the individual accuracy gain. The analysis highlights the importance of system‐level evaluation and suggests that pre‐AI elicitation, diversified AI inputs, and audits of correlated omissions can help preserve the redundancy benefit of multiple assessments.

authors: Rupak Biswas; Santhosh Juvvaka

abstract: ABSTRACT This review assesses Daniel Berliner's Learning from the Public, which treats the processing of citizen input as a neglected stage of participation. Its typology of processing is valuable for research and practice. However, the evidence is illustrative; the book does not separate weak capacity from unwillingness to listen, and thin coverage of the global South limits its general claims.

title: Growing, but Not Necessarily Showing: Pregnancy in Remote Versus In‐Person Contexts
authors: Aashna M. Waiwood; Tammy D. Allen; Alyssa M. Lezcano; Joseph Regina
affiliations: U.S. Department of Defense Washington DC USA; University of South Florida Tampa Florida USA; Rutgers University Camden New Jersey USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Pregnancy is a stigmatized state in the workplace, and research has increasingly documented the unique experience of being pregnant at work, including difficulties with pregnancy disclosure. Theory and research seemingly take as a given that women's pregnancies are visible or that they become visible. Moreover, visibility appears crucial to explaining pregnancy‐related experiences, behaviors, and treatment. However, working remotely alters the presumed inevitability of visibility. Based on qualitative and quantitative data, we explore how working remotely corresponds with women's disclosure and postdisclosure pregnancy‐related perceptions, decisions, and experiences. Findings demonstrate that time working remotely is associated with greater perceptions of disclosure control, disclosure to a narrower network, delayed disclosure timing, and reduced need to disclose for transparency purposes. In the postdisclosure period, time working remotely is related to reduced conspicuousness of the “unseemly” pregnant body and its symptoms, or fewer physical “reminders,” of one's pregnancy and pregnancy‐related behaviors, corresponding with reduced awareness, addressing, and comments (often invasive in nature) on one's pregnant status by others. Results support the importance of accounting for stigma visibility and obtrusiveness in existing theories and have implications for the use of remote work or other visibility‐linked strategies to address pregnancy experiences.

title: Can Workplace Creativity Increase Positive Affect Through Absorption? The Moderating Roles of Negative Affect and Competitive Climate
authors: March L. To; Gillian Yeo; Cynthia D. Fisher
affiliations: School of Management, College of Business and Law RMIT University Melbourne Australia; University of Western Australia Perth Australia; Bond University Gold Coast Australia
abstract: ABSTRACT Workplace creativity is often studied as an outcome influenced by employees' affective states. There is growing interest in the potential for creative activity to improve positive affect, but there is insufficient knowledge about when or why such activity may change how employees feel at work. We draw on affect regulation theory to consider the mechanisms and boundary conditions involved in the relationship between creative process engagement (CPE) and changes in positive affect. We suggest that engaging in creative processes at work has the potential to increase positive affect through increased task absorption. However, our framework highlights that these effects of CPE are contingent on two factors: the accompanying negative affect and the surrounding competitive climate for creativity. We develop progressive support for our predictions in a laboratory experiment followed by a field experience sampling study. The laboratory study found that CPE increased positive affect through greater task absorption when negative affect was high. The field study tested and supported our full model, with competitive climate for creativity impacting the moderated‐mediated relationship, such that it weakened the CPE × negative affect interactive effect on increasing positive affect via task absorption.

title: Standardization participation and exploitative and exploratory innovation
authors: Yong Zhang; Mengli Zhao; Shibin Sheng; Jinxin Liu
affiliations: School of Management, Jinan University , ,; Economics and Management School, Wuhan University , ,; Research Center for Organizational Marketing, Wuhan University , ,; Collat School of Business, University of Alabama at Birmingham , , ,; School of Management, Huazhong University of Science and Technology , ,
abstract: Purpose Firms participate in the development of technical standards to coordinate interfaces and reduce uncertainty, yet the implications of such participation for the direction of firms’ technological search remain underexplored. This study aims to examine how standardization participation shapes exploitative and exploratory innovation and how institutional conditions shape these relationships. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a firm–year panel of 486 publicly listed Chinese manufacturing firms from 2011 to 2020 to examine the relationships between standardization participation and exploitative and exploratory innovation, together with the moderating effects of institutional conditions. The complementary analysis leverages China’s 2015 standardization reform as a quasi-natural experiment. By encouraging and facilitating firms’ engagement in standardization, the reform provides a complementary setting for examining the innovation consequences of greater standardization engagement. Findings Standardization participation is positively associated with exploitative innovation but negatively associated with exploratory innovation. Legal effectiveness strengthens the positive association with exploitative innovation and the negative association with exploratory innovation. Political connections mitigate the negative association with exploratory innovation. The complementary difference-in-differences analysis shows that, following the 2015 standardization reform, firms in covered industries exhibited higher exploitative innovation and lower exploratory innovation relative to firms in non-covered industries. Originality/value This study extends research on standardization participation by showing that its innovation consequences are directionally asymmetric rather than uniformly positive. It contributes to operations management research by integrating operational coordination and technological search perspectives, showing that coordination and knowledge benefits can coexist with path-shaping consequences that favor familiar technological trajectories. A routine-based path-dependence account explains this pattern. The study further shows that legal effectiveness and political connections differentially condition these directional consequences.

title: Unions and Artificial Intelligence: Negotiating Technological Change in the Norwegian Financial Sector
authors: Fredrik Bakkemo Kostøl; Sander I. Harefallet; Marcus B. Monsvoll
affiliations: Department of Industrial Economics and Technology Management Norwegian University of Science and Technology Trondheim Norway; Norwegian University of Science and Technology Trondheim Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is spreading rapidly in the workplace, yet evidence on how unions respond to and shape its adoption remains limited. This article examines union engagement with AI in the Norwegian financial sector. Using a mixed‐methods design, we combine register analysis, a survey of union representatives and a case study of Microsoft Copilot's roll‐out in a major Nordic financial corporation. The register analysis shows a modest but robust positive association between unionisation and occupational AI exposure, indicating that unionised workers are somewhat more concentrated in occupations whose tasks are potentially affected by AI. Qualitative evidence shows that union representatives adopt a pragmatic stance: They accept AI's potential benefits but emphasise governance rules, inclusive training and the protection of employee interests. In practice, union engagement centres on conditions of use, particularly monitoring, data use and competence development, whereas core adoption decisions remain largely management‐driven. The findings highlight a central limit of institutionalised worker participation: Involvement in implementation does not necessarily extend to control over technological choices or the distribution of productivity gains.

title: Domestic Tariffs and Consumer Welfare in Developing Countries: Evidence From India
authors: Jerónimo Callejas; Chirantan Chatterjee; Debi Prasad Mohapatra
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst Massachusetts USA; Department of Economics University of Sussex Business School Brighton UK
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the welfare consequences of industrial policies aimed at boosting domestic manufacturing in developing countries, focusing on the Indian government's tariff policy for mobile handset production. We develop a structural model of India's mobile handset industry, where firms endogenously decide supply chain alternatives, product sets, and prices. Our counterfactual simulations indicate that the status quo import tariff on ready‐to‐use handsets significantly increases local assembly operations. However, a lower tariff of around 8% would maintain similar assembly levels and significantly enhance consumer surplus. An additional input import tariff on handset components discourages firms from relocating operations to India, potentially undermining the policy's goal.

title:
Intended and Unintended Consequences of the
                    <scp>FASB</scp>
                    's Revised Liability Definition: Evidence From Constructive Obligations
authors: Shannon M. Garavaglia; Cassie A. Mongold; Brian J. White
affiliations: Accounting Department, Katz Graduate School of Business University of Pittsburgh Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA; Department of Accountancy, Gies College of Business University of Illinois at Urbana‐Champaign Champaign Illinois USA; Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management, Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Ithaca New York USA
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine consequences of the FASB's recent revision to the liability definition, which repositions “present obligation” to emphasize obligation existence over future economic outflows as the primary defining characteristic of a liability. The new definition achieves its intended effect: Individuals place greater weight on present obligations and less weight on future outflows when identifying liabilities. However, individuals are also substantially less likely to identify constructive liabilities arising from customary business practices—a result arguably inconsistent with the FASB's intent. Additional experiments establish that differential emphasis drives this effect and that individuals apply a legal standard when assessing whether an obligation exists—one that customary practice does not meet. We also find the new definition biases experienced accounting professionals toward nonrecognition and provides a basis for resisting future standards proposing the recognition of constructive liabilities. Interviews with professional investors reveal strong demand for information about constructive liabilities, suggesting a misalignment between the revised definition and users' information needs.

title: Blood is Still Thicker Than Water: A Response to Lin’s Reappraisal and Reflections on Historical Political Economy
authors: YUHUA WANG
affiliations: Harvard University
abstract: A recent reappraisal by Lin expands Wang’s (2022, American Political Science Review 116, 896–910) dataset and questions the robustness of its main finding. In this response, I clarify broader challenges of measurement, case selection, and inference in historical political economy. I show that my original finding—that kinship-network concentration is negatively associated with support for state-building reforms—remains robust across multiple coding strategies. I also acknowledge that two high-leverage cases, the Lü brothers, matter for inference; rather than treating them as removable anomalies, I argue that their extreme values are theoretically meaningful features of kinship-network structure. Finally, I engage Lin’s regional interpretation and show that regional status competition does not account for the observed relationship once measurement and estimation issues are addressed. More broadly, this exchange illustrates how transparent measurement and sustained dialogue between quantitative and qualitative evidence can generate cumulative knowledge from fragmentary historical archives.

title: Do Politicians’ Errors in Understanding Public Opinion Persist When They Encounter Individual Constituents?
authors: JACK LUCAS; LIOR SHEFFER; NOAM TITELMAN
affiliations: University of Calgary; Tel Aviv University
abstract: When thinking about public opinion, politicians commonly exhibit three general perceptual errors: a tendency to overestimate their constituents’ conservatism ( conservative bias ), a tendency to hold more accurate knowledge of privileged constituents than constituents in general ( privilege bias ), and a tendency to overestimate how much their constituents share their views ( projection bias ). Studies documenting these patterns invariably rely on assessing politicians’ perceptions of aggregated public opinion. In practice, however, politicians heavily prioritize and rely on the opinions of individual constituents, raising concerns about the external validity of these findings. Thus, in this article, we explore whether politicians’ common perceptual errors persist when they think about specific individual constituents, rather than aggregate public opinion. We assign more than 1,400 Canadian politicians to predict the ideology and issue positions of more than 4,000 randomly generated citizen profiles that vary by a host of salient sociodemographic and political factors. We then compare their evaluations to estimates of these citizens’ real-life positions drawn from a general population survey. We find that politicians do not exhibit conservative bias or privilege bias when making inferences about individual constituents. However, even when thinking about individual constituents, projection bias persists, and the perception errors it creates are amplified when politicians are more similar to their constituents. We discuss the implications of these findings for theories of political representation.

title: Conspiracy theory communication framing and support for antidemocratic behavior
authors: Frances Cayton; Courtney Blackington
affiliations: Center on Democracy, Development, and the Rule of Law Stanford University Stanford California USA; Department of Political Science University of Pittsburgh Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA
abstract: Abstract Many politicians use conspiracy theories (CTs) to win electoral support and justify antidemocratic policies. How do individuals evaluate this strategy? We theorize and show that variation in CT communication frames affects individuals’ willingness to endorse antidemocratic policies and politicians. Politicians who explicitly appeal to a CT earn greater support for antidemocratic behavior than those using implicit appeals. However, this effect primarily occurs for novel CTs lacking partisan cues. Over time, as CTs become more politicized, they lose their mobilizational capacity and can reduce support for CT‐wielding politicians—even among co‐partisans. Three preregistered survey experiments surrounding the 2023 parliamentary and 2025 presidential elections in Poland, and survey data from 21 countries, provide empirical support for our theory. Ultimately, we show that CTs alone are not always enough to justify attacks on democratic norms and institutions to the public.
